title: How to Improve Infant Digestion Naturally: Safe Tips
summary: Get practical advice on how to improve infant digestion naturally with safe, gentle tips for feeding, soothing, and knowing when to call your pediatrician.
body_markdown:
There’s plenty of advice about baby digestion, but not all of it is specific to your child—or backed by clear evidence. A probiotic that has been studied for one strain or concern may not work the same way for another baby. So how to improve infant digestion naturally is less about finding a universal remedy and more about understanding what your baby needs. Start by looking at feeding, stool patterns, comfort, and overall wellbeing. In this guide, you’ll find practical steps that may help, plus guidance on probiotics, prebiotics, and synbiotics. You’ll also learn when to check with your pediatrician and how to recognize symptoms that need prompt care.


## Key Takeaways


- **Keep care simple and age-appropriate** : Follow feeding cues, try gentle comfort measures while your baby is awake, and check with your pediatrician before changing feeds or offering extra fluids.
- **Track what’s typical for your baby** : Note feeds, diapers, stools, and when discomfort occurs to help your pediatrician assess any patterns.
- **Ask before trying a remedy or supplement** : Products vary in ingredients and evidence, so discuss the specific option with your pediatrician. Seek prompt care for green vomit, blood in the stool, or fewer wet diapers.


## How to Support Infant Digestion Naturally


A baby’s digestion develops over time, and occasional gas or changes in stool are common. Start with age-appropriate feeding and gentle comfort measures. If symptoms persist, worsen, or concern you, your pediatrician can help you decide what to try next.


### Use age-appropriate feeding and gentle comfort measures


For babies under about 6 months, breast milk or correctly prepared formula usually provides the fluids they need. Don’t offer extra water unless your pediatrician recommends it. When your baby is ready for solids, usually around 6 months, introduce suitable foods gradually. If constipation is a concern, ask whether pureed pears or prunes are appropriate for your baby’s age and symptoms.


A gentle tummy massage or slowly moving your baby’s legs in a bicycling motion may help them settle. Use light pressure while your baby is awake, and stop if they seem uncomfortable. A warm bath or cuddling can also be soothing, though comfort measures may not address the cause of ongoing symptoms.[A-Z Pediatrics offers guidance on gentle massage and feeding-related approaches](https://a-zpeds.com/handling-common-newborn-digestive-issues-from-gas-to-constipation) .


### Check with a clinician before trying “natural” remedies


“Natural” products are not automatically safe or suitable for infants. Herbal preparations, gripe water, and supplements can contain different ingredients, and recommendations may depend on your baby’s age, symptoms, and health history. Check with your pediatrician before giving one, particularly to a newborn. It’s also wise to ask before changing formula, feeding routines, or your diet while breastfeeding.


If you’re considering a probiotic, ask about the specific strain, the evidence for your baby’s age and concern, and any possible risks. Research on one strain or symptom doesn’t mean every product will have the same effect. Your clinician can help determine whether feeding support or a medical assessment is needed. If home care hasn’t helped after a few days, or symptoms are getting worse,[contact your healthcare provider for advice](https://a-zpeds.com/handling-common-newborn-digestive-issues-from-gas-to-constipation) .


## What Does Normal Infant Digestion Look Like?


### Expect variation in stool frequency, color, gas, and spit-up


There isn’t one schedule or appearance that’s right for every baby. How often your baby poops, and what their stool looks like, can depend on their age and whether they’re breastfed, formula-fed, or both. Yellow, brown, and green stools are common. Your baby’s usual pattern and overall wellbeing can offer more useful context than a single diaper.


Gas and small spit-ups are also common in infancy. If your baby is feeding comfortably and seems well between feeds, occasional gas or spit-up may be part of normal development. Keep an eye on changes that persist or concern you, and ask your pediatrician what’s typical for your baby.[Kate Farms’ overview of common digestive issues](https://katefarms.com/resources/discover/article/5-digestive-issues-to-look-out-for) offers more context on symptoms families may notice.


### Know that grunting or straining with soft stools can be normal


Some babies grunt, turn red, or strain before passing stool. When the stool is soft, those efforts alone don’t necessarily mean your baby is constipated. Babies are still learning to coordinate the muscles involved in having a bowel movement, and the process can look more dramatic than it is.


Hard, dry stools or painful bowel movements are different and are worth discussing with your pediatrician. The[American Academy of Pediatrics’ guidance on infant abdominal pain](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/health-issues/conditions/abdominal/Pages/Abdominal-Pains-in-Infants.aspx) notes that hard, infrequent stools can be a sign of constipation. If you’re uncertain, describe what you’re seeing rather than trying to diagnose it yourself. Your clinician can consider your baby’s age, feeding, and usual stool pattern.


### Notice whether fussiness is occasional or follows a pattern


Fussiness happens, and an unsettled stretch doesn’t automatically point to a digestive problem. Notice when it occurs: during a feed, soon afterward, or around the same time each day. You can jot down feeds, diapers, spit-up, and crying for a few days if you’re seeing a repeated pattern.


That information can help your pediatrician understand what has changed and whether anything needs attention. Note whether your baby settles between episodes, feeds as usual, and has their typical number of wet diapers.[Mead Johnson’s overview of infant digestive issues](https://hcp.meadjohnson.com/nutrition-health/digestive-issues) describes fussiness and gassiness among signs that may accompany digestive discomfort. If symptoms persist, worsen, or make feeding difficult, check in with your clinician.


## Which Digestive Symptoms Should You Watch For?


Gas, spit-up, crying, and changing stools are common in babies. A symptom is more useful to track when you consider how often it happens, whether your baby seems uncomfortable, and whether feeding or diaper habits have changed. Write down what you notice and when it occurs so you can share a clear picture with your pediatrician.


### Recognize gas, reflux, colic, constipation, and diarrhea


Gas may cause burping, passing wind, or brief fussiness. Reflux often looks like milk coming back up after a feed. Spit-up is common, but talk with your pediatrician if it comes with feeding difficulty, persistent discomfort, or concerns about weight gain. The[Kate Farms guide to digestive issues in children](https://katefarms.com/resources/discover/article/5-digestive-issues-to-look-out-for) outlines signs associated with reflux and indigestion.


Colic usually refers to repeated, prolonged crying in an otherwise healthy baby. Constipation is more often marked by hard, dry stools or pain when passing them, not just fewer bowel movements. Straining with a soft stool can be normal. Diarrhea is a noticeable change to looser or more frequent stools. Since babies’ usual patterns vary, focus on what has changed for yours.


### Watch for discomfort, feeding trouble, or dehydration


Notice whether your baby regularly cries, arches, or pulls away during feeds, or seems uncomfortable afterward. Occasional fussiness is common, but ongoing distress or trouble feeding deserves a conversation with your pediatrician. Keep track of how long feeds last, how much your baby takes, and whether discomfort follows a particular feed or time of day. The[Mead Johnson guide to infant digestive issues](https://hcp.meadjohnson.com/nutrition-health/digestive-issues) also lists fussiness, gas, and constipation as symptoms to watch for.


Pay attention to wet diapers, too. Fewer wet diapers than usual, a dry mouth, or unusual sleepiness can be signs of dehydration. Contact your pediatrician promptly if you notice these changes, especially if your baby is feeding less or has vomiting or diarrhea.


### Spot red flags: green vomit, blood in stool, or fewer wet diapers


Green vomit, rather than ordinary milky spit-up, needs urgent medical assessment. Contact your pediatrician right away or seek urgent care, especially if your baby also seems very unwell, has a swollen belly, or cannot keep feeds down.


Call your pediatrician if you see blood in your baby’s stool, even if it is only a small amount. The[American Academy of Pediatrics guidance on infant abdominal pain](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/health-issues/conditions/abdominal/Pages/Abdominal-Pains-in-Infants.aspx) advises parents to report blood in stool. Fewer wet diapers can also signal dehydration. If your baby is difficult to wake or appears seriously unwell, seek urgent care. When you call, share when the symptom started, how often it has happened, and any changes in feeding or diapers.


## How Can Feeding Practices Support Digestion?


Feeding routines can sometimes ease discomfort, but there’s no single approach that works for every baby. Try one practical adjustment at a time and notice how your baby responds. If feeding is painful, difficult, or causing ongoing concern, your pediatrician or a lactation consultant can help you decide what to try next.


### Check latch, positioning, and milk transfer when breastfeeding


A comfortable latch and supportive position can help your baby feed effectively. Aim to bring your baby close, with their body facing you and their mouth open wide at the breast. You may hear or see swallowing during a feed. Persistent nipple pain, difficulty staying latched, or concern that your baby isn’t getting enough milk are good reasons to ask for help. A lactation consultant or pediatrician can observe a feed and check positioning and milk transfer. These details can be hard to assess on your own, so you don’t have to figure them out from a checklist.[Coast Pediatrics shares guidance on breastfeeding latch and positioning](https://www.coastpediatrics.com/natural-remedies-for-gastrointestinal-problems) .


### Pace bottle-feeds and choose a suitable nipple flow


For bottle-feeding, hold your baby close in a semi-upright position and keep the bottle angled so milk flows steadily. Pause when your baby does, and avoid encouraging them to finish if they turn away or seem full. A nipple that flows too quickly may lead some babies to gulp or cough; one that flows too slowly may make feeding frustrating. Watch how your baby feeds, and ask your pediatrician if you’re unsure whether the nipple flow is suitable.[A-Z Pediatrics describes paced bottle-feeding and nipple flow](https://a-zpeds.com/handling-common-newborn-digestive-issues-from-gas-to-constipation) .


### Follow hunger and fullness cues; ask about feed size or frequency


Early hunger cues can include turning toward the breast or bottle, bringing hands to the mouth, or becoming more alert. Slowing down, turning away, or closing the mouth can mean your baby needs a pause or has had enough. Cues and feeding needs vary, especially as babies grow, so a general schedule may not fit your child. If you’re unsure how much or how often to offer, ask your pediatrician for guidance based on your baby’s age, growth, and feeding pattern. Responding to cues can help make feeds calmer without pressuring your baby to finish.


### Burp during or after feeds; hold baby upright briefly while awake


Some babies seem more comfortable after releasing swallowed air. If your baby appears unsettled, pause to burp during a feed or gently pat their back afterward. You can also hold your baby upright briefly after feeding while they’re awake and supervised. These steps may help, but babies differ, and not every baby needs to burp after every feed. Upright holding is only for awake time: when it’s time to sleep, place your baby on their back on a firm, flat surface.[Smiles Hospitals offers tips for burping and post-feed comfort](https://gastroenterology.smileshospitals.com/ways-to-improve-your-babys-digestive-system) .


### Don’t change formula or restrict a breastfeeding parent’s diet without medical advice


If you think formula or a food in your diet may be affecting your baby, talk with your pediatrician before making changes. Switching formulas or removing foods from a breastfeeding parent’s meals may not address the cause, and making several changes at once can make it harder to identify what helps. A clinician can review your baby’s symptoms, feeding, and growth, then advise whether a change makes sense and how to do it safely. Contact your pediatrician about persistent symptoms, feeding difficulties, blood in the stool, or poor weight gain.[Coast Pediatrics advises consulting a healthcare professional before changing feeding practices](https://www.coastpediatrics.com/natural-remedies-for-gastrointestinal-problems) .


## Which Gentle Soothing Strategies Are Safe?


When your baby seems uncomfortable, it’s natural to want to help. Gentle touch, a cuddle, or a change of position may help your baby settle, but these steps don’t identify or treat the cause of digestive symptoms. Try one calm approach at a time while your baby is awake and you can supervise. Stop if your baby cries harder, resists, or seems uncomfortable.


Keep an eye on the bigger picture, too. Notice whether your baby is feeding as usual, having their typical number of wet diapers, and behaving normally between fussy periods. Contact your pediatrician if discomfort keeps returning, affects feeding, or comes with symptoms such as persistent vomiting, blood in the stool, or fewer wet diapers.


Sleep safety is essential, even when your baby has gas or spits up. For every sleep, place your baby on their back on a firm, flat surface. The[American Academy of Pediatrics’ safe sleep guidance](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/sleep/Pages/a-parents-guide-to-safe-sleep.aspx) explains how to create a safer sleep space.


### Massage baby’s tummy or move their legs gently while they’re awake


If your baby seems gassy, try a light tummy massage while they’re awake and calm. Use your fingertips to make slow, gentle circles on their abdomen. You can also move their legs softly in a bicycling motion. Keep the movements easy, and stop if your baby resists or becomes upset. Avoid pressing on the belly, especially just after a feed.


These comfort measures may not help every baby, and that’s okay. A[pediatric clinic’s guide to newborn digestive issues](https://a-zpeds.com/handling-common-newborn-digestive-issues-from-gas-to-constipation) describes gentle massage as one option to try. If your baby’s belly looks swollen or feels hard, or you notice other concerning symptoms, contact your pediatrician rather than continuing to massage.


### Soothe with supervised tummy time, a warm bath, or cuddling


While your baby is awake, supervised tummy time can offer a change of position and support their development. Stay close and use a firm, clear surface. If your baby becomes sleepy, move them to their sleep space and place them on their back. The CDC’s tummy time guidance offers practical tips for adding short sessions to the day.


Cuddling or a comfortably warm bath may also help your baby relax. During bath time, keep a hand on your baby and never leave them alone near water, even briefly. These options are for comfort, not treatment. Choose what your baby seems to enjoy, and stop if they become more upset.


### Keep sleep safe: place baby on their back on a firm, flat surface


Place your baby on their back for every sleep, even if they have gas, reflux, or spit up. Use a firm, flat, separate sleep surface, such as a crib or bassinet, with a fitted sheet. Keep pillows, loose blankets, wedges, and positioners out of the sleep space. Don’t raise one end of the mattress or use an inclined sleeper.


If spit-up or reflux is disrupting feeds or your baby’s growth, ask your pediatrician for guidance. Don’t change your baby’s sleep position to try to manage digestive discomfort. The[AAP’s safe sleep recommendations](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/sleep/Pages/a-parents-guide-to-safe-sleep.aspx) explain why back sleeping on a firm, flat surface matters.


### Remember that soothing may ease discomfort without treating its cause


A massage, cuddle, or warm bath may help your baby settle in the moment, but it can’t tell you what’s causing the discomfort. Gas, spit-up, and fussiness can have different explanations, and fussiness alone doesn’t point to a specific digestive problem.


If symptoms keep returning, interfere with feeding, or worry you, note when they happen and discuss them with your pediatrician. A short record of feeds, diapers, spit-up, and stool changes can help you describe what you’ve noticed. Soothing can be part of caring for your baby, while a clinician can help assess persistent symptoms and recommend next steps.


## How Does Hydration Affect Infant Digestion?


Hydration needs change as your baby grows. In the first months, breast milk or correctly prepared formula provides the fluid and nourishment babies need. Once solids begin, your pediatrician can help you decide whether to offer small sips of water. If you’re worried about your baby’s fluids or digestion, ask for guidance before trying a home remedy.


### Use breast milk or formula as the main fluid for the first 6 months


For about the first six months, breast milk or infant formula should be your baby’s main source of hydration and nutrition. Both provide fluid along with nutrients that support growth. The Gerber Medical guide to healthy digestion also identifies breast milk or formula as the primary source during this stage.


If you use formula, prepare it exactly as directed. Adding extra water can change its nutrient balance and may be unsafe. If your baby seems unusually thirsty, has fewer wet diapers, or is feeding differently, contact your pediatrician rather than offering water without advice.


### Ask when to offer small amounts of water after solids begin


When your baby is ready for solid foods, usually around six months, ask your pediatrician whether to offer small sips of water with meals. Water can help your baby practice drinking from a cup, but breast milk or formula should remain the main source of fluids and nutrition.[A-Z Pediatrics’ overview of common newborn digestive issues](https://a-zpeds.com/handling-common-newborn-digestive-issues-from-gas-to-constipation) recommends introducing small amounts after solids begin without replacing milk feeds.


Your baby’s age, health, and feeding pattern all matter, so there’s no need to rush. If constipation or another digestive concern is prompting you to consider water, check with your pediatrician first.


### Watch for dehydration, such as fewer wet diapers or unusual sleepiness


Fewer wet diapers than usual, a dry mouth, or unusual sleepiness can be signs of dehydration. The[American Academy of Pediatrics’ HealthyChildren.org guidance](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/health-issues/conditions/abdominal/Pages/Abdominal-Pains-in-Infants.aspx) lists these signs among concerns to watch for.


Diaper patterns vary with age and feeding, so pay attention to what’s typical for your baby. Contact your pediatrician promptly if you notice a clear change, or your baby is feeding poorly or seems unwell. If your baby is difficult to wake or symptoms seem severe, seek urgent medical care. Don’t wait to see whether offering extra water helps.


### Don’t offer extra water or juice unless your pediatrician recommends it


It may seem like water or juice could help when your baby is constipated or uncomfortable, but extra fluids aren’t right for every infant. Too much water can interfere with the nutrition your baby gets from breast milk or formula, and juice may not be appropriate for their age or symptoms.[University Hospitals’ guidance on children’s gut health](https://www.uhhospitals.org/blog/articles/2017/03/6-ways-to-boost-your-childs-gut-health) recommends checking with a pediatrician before giving an infant extra water or juice.


Don’t dilute formula or use juice as a home remedy unless your baby’s clinician recommends it. When you call, share feeding amounts, wet diaper patterns, and any stool changes. That information can help your pediatrician suggest a safe next step.


## Which Foods Are Appropriate Once Solids Begin?


Starting solids is about helping your baby learn to eat, one small taste at a time. Breast milk or formula remains an important source of nutrition as you introduce foods. Follow your baby’s readiness and cues, choose safe textures, and ask your pediatrician if you’re unsure what’s right for your child.


### Start solids when baby shows readiness, usually around 6 months


Most babies are ready to try solid foods at around 6 months. Look for signs of developmental readiness: your baby can hold their head steady, sit upright with support, and swallow food rather than push it out with their tongue. They may also lean toward food or open their mouth when you offer a taste. Age alone isn’t the whole picture, so check with your pediatrician if you’re unsure whether your baby is ready. The[CDC’s guidance on starting solid foods](https://www.cdc.gov/infant-toddler-nutrition/foods-and-drinks/when-what-and-how-to-introduce-solid-foods.html) offers more detail on readiness and how to begin.


### Offer varied, age-appropriate foods and textures gradually


Start with a small amount of soft food in a texture your baby can manage, then gradually offer different flavors and textures. Mashed vegetables, soft fruit, and iron-rich foods are examples to discuss with your pediatrician as you plan early meals. As your baby develops eating skills, you can adjust the texture while continuing to supervise closely. Avoid foods that are hard, round, sticky, or difficult to chew, since they may pose a choking risk. There’s no need to pressure your baby to finish a serving. Exploring food by looking, touching, and tasting is part of learning. Gerber Medical’s guide to supporting a healthy gut also recommends introducing varied, age-appropriate foods and textures gradually.


### Ask whether pears or prunes suit your baby’s age and symptoms


Pears or prunes may be suggested for babies with hard stools, but they aren’t the right solution for every baby or every digestive concern. What’s appropriate depends on your baby’s age, feeding stage, symptoms, and overall health. Ask your pediatrician before using these foods to address constipation, especially if your baby has ongoing discomfort or has only recently started solids. If your clinician recommends them, serve them in a texture that’s safe for your baby’s current eating skills.[A-Z Pediatrics discusses pears and prunes](https://a-zpeds.com/handling-common-newborn-digestive-issues-from-gas-to-constipation) as possible options for babies experiencing constipation.


### Introduce foods safely; discuss suspected allergies with your pediatrician


Offer new foods in a safe texture and supervise your baby while they eat. Common allergenic foods don’t generally need to be delayed once a baby is ready for solids, but ask your pediatrician for guidance if your baby has severe eczema, a known food allergy, or another risk factor. If you notice a possible reaction, stop offering that food and contact your pediatrician. Seek emergency care for severe symptoms such as trouble breathing or swelling of the face or tongue. Keep notes on what your baby ate and what symptoms followed; that information can help your clinician advise you on next steps.


## Can Probiotics, Prebiotics, or Synbiotics Help?


Probiotics, prebiotics, and synbiotics are not interchangeable, and none is a guaranteed fix for gas, fussiness, or changes in stool. Whether a supplement may be appropriate depends on your baby’s age, health, symptoms, and the product’s specific ingredients. Your pediatrician can help you consider the evidence and decide whether it makes sense for your child.


### Learn how they differ and why effects depend on specific strains


Probiotics are live microorganisms that may provide a health benefit when consumed in adequate amounts. Prebiotics are ingredients that certain microorganisms can use. Synbiotics combine probiotics and prebiotics in one product. These terms cover many different ingredients, so findings about one product do not automatically apply to another.


Research often focuses on a particular strain and a specific situation. For example,[L. reuteri DSM 17938](https://www.coastpediatrics.com/natural-remedies-for-gastrointestinal-problems) has been studied for colic in breastfed infants, but the reported effect was not observed in formula-fed infants. The strain, your baby’s circumstances, and the reason for considering a product all matter.


### Ask your pediatrician about evidence, age guidance, ingredients, and safety


Before giving your baby a probiotic, prebiotic, or synbiotic, ask your pediatrician whether it is appropriate and what evidence supports its use for the concern you’re seeing. Recommendations may depend on your baby’s age, health history, feeding, and symptoms. Your clinician can also review the product’s ingredients and directions, including whether it is intended for infants.


Bring the package or a clear photo of the label to your appointment. Ask what changes to look for, how long to use the product, and when to stop or check back.[Pediatric guidance on infant digestive issues](https://a-zpeds.com/handling-common-newborn-digestive-issues-from-gas-to-constipation) can help you understand why it’s worth discussing evidence, age recommendations, and safety before adding a supplement.


### Ask about Bifidobacterium and named strains, not broad claims


Bifidobacterium is a group of bacteria that includes types studied in infant health. However, the word “Bifidobacterium” alone does not tell you which strain a product contains or what evidence applies to it. Ask your pediatrician to review the full strain name, the amount included, and any other ingredients.


This gives you more useful information than a general label claim such as “supports gut health.” The[University Hospitals guide to children’s gut health](https://www.uhhospitals.org/blog/articles/2017/03/6-ways-to-boost-your-childs-gut-health) also advises asking about specific strains, since effects may differ. A clear label can help you and your clinician discuss what’s in a product without assuming that all probiotics work alike.


### Don’t use supplements instead of feeding support or medical care


A supplement should not replace feeding support or an evaluation of ongoing symptoms. If your baby seems uncomfortable, a clinician may look at latch, bottle-feeding technique, feeding amounts, or other possible causes. A supplement may not address the reason your baby is having trouble.


Contact your pediatrician if symptoms persist, feeding becomes difficult, or you notice signs such as fewer wet diapers, blood in the stool, or unusual sleepiness.[A-Z Pediatrics’ guidance on newborn digestive issues](https://a-zpeds.com/handling-common-newborn-digestive-issues-from-gas-to-constipation) recommends seeking medical advice when home measures do not help. Your pediatrician can suggest next steps and discuss whether a supplement has a role.


## Which Remedies Should You Avoid?


When your baby seems uncomfortable, it’s natural to look for something that might help. But infants can respond differently to products intended for older children or adults. Before trying a remedy, check with your pediatrician, especially if your baby is very young or has ongoing symptoms.


### Avoid herbal teas, gripe water, laxatives, or diluted formula unless advised


Herbal teas such as chamomile or fennel may sound gentle, but their effects in infants aren’t well studied, and products can contain different ingredients. Gripe water also varies by brand. Ask your pediatrician before giving either, even if a product is marketed for babies.[Coast Pediatrics recommends discussing herbal remedies with a healthcare provider](https://www.coastpediatrics.com/natural-remedies-for-gastrointestinal-problems) .


Don’t give a laxative unless your baby’s clinician recommends a specific product and dose. Prepare formula exactly as directed on the package; adding extra water can interfere with your baby’s nutrition and health. If you’re concerned about constipation, feeding, or your baby’s comfort, ask your pediatrician what to do rather than trying these remedies on your own.


### Check age guidance and safety before giving supplements or home remedies


A product that’s suitable for an older child may not be appropriate for an infant. Supplements and home remedies can differ in ingredients, strength, and age guidance, so check with your pediatrician before giving your baby a probiotic, prebiotic, herbal product, or other remedy. Bring the package or a clear photo of the ingredient list to your appointment.


If a remedy hasn’t helped, don’t increase the amount or combine it with another product without medical advice. Persistent symptoms may need a closer look, and your pediatrician can suggest options suited to your baby.[A-Z Pediatrics recommends contacting a healthcare provider](https://a-zpeds.com/handling-common-newborn-digestive-issues-from-gas-to-constipation) if home remedies don’t seem to help after a few days.


### Never use an inclined sleeper or put baby down to sleep upright


You can hold your baby upright briefly after a feed while they’re awake and supervised. For sleep, always place them on their back on a firm, flat surface. Don’t use an inclined sleeper, wedge, or positioner, and don’t leave your baby to sleep in a car seat or other sitting device after travel.


These safe-sleep steps still apply if your baby spits up or has reflux. The[American Academy of Pediatrics’ safe-sleep guidance](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/sleep/Pages/A-Parents-Guide-to-Safe-Sleep.aspx) explains how to create a safer sleep space. If reflux is affecting your baby’s feeding or comfort, ask your pediatrician about ways to manage it while keeping sleep safe.


## When Should You Call a Pediatrician?


Many changes in a baby’s digestion are temporary, but certain symptoms deserve prompt medical advice. If you’re worried or your baby seems unlike themselves, call your pediatrician and explain what you’ve noticed. You don’t need to figure out the cause before reaching out.


### Seek urgent care for green or bloody vomit, breathing trouble, or severe lethargy


Get urgent medical care if your baby vomits green fluid or blood, has trouble breathing, or is unusually difficult to wake or respond. If your baby is struggling to breathe or is unresponsive, call emergency services.


These symptoms can signal a serious problem that needs prompt evaluation. The American Academy of Pediatrics’[guidance on abdominal pain in infants](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/health-issues/conditions/abdominal/Pages/Abdominal-Pains-in-Infants.aspx) advises seeking urgent care for green or bloody vomit and severe lethargy. When you contact a clinician, share when the symptom started, how often it has happened, and whether you’ve noticed other changes.


### Call promptly for persistent vomiting or diarrhea, feeding refusal, dehydration signs, or fever in a young infant


Contact your pediatrician promptly if your baby has repeated vomiting or diarrhea, refuses feeds, or shows possible dehydration. Signs can include fewer wet diapers than usual, a dry mouth, or unusual sleepiness. For a baby younger than 3 months, a temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher needs prompt medical attention. Follow your clinician’s advice about taking your baby’s temperature and where to seek care.


Babies can lose fluids quickly, so don’t wait for symptoms to worsen before asking for help.[HealthyChildren.org’s advice for infant abdominal symptoms](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/health-issues/conditions/abdominal/Pages/Abdominal-Pains-in-Infants.aspx) includes persistent vomiting or diarrhea, feeding refusal, dehydration signs, and fever in a young infant among reasons to contact a clinician.


### Discuss ongoing discomfort, hard stools, or poor weight gain


Bring up symptoms that keep returning or seem to affect your baby’s comfort, feeding, or growth. These may include distress around bowel movements, persistently hard stools, or concern that your baby isn’t gaining weight as expected. Your pediatrician can consider your baby’s age, feeding pattern, growth, and symptoms when deciding whether an evaluation or a change in care is needed.


Avoid giving laxatives or other remedies unless your clinician recommends them.[Kate Farms’ overview of digestive issues in children](https://katefarms.com/resources/discover/article/5-digestive-issues-to-look-out-for) also recommends discussing ongoing discomfort, hard stools, and poor weight gain with a healthcare professional. If symptoms worsen suddenly or appear alongside urgent warning signs, seek care sooner.


### Track feeds, diapers, and symptoms to describe what has changed


A few notes can help you explain what’s happening during a call or appointment. Record when and how much your baby feeds, wet and dirty diaper counts, stool consistency, and any spit-up or vomiting. Note when discomfort occurs, your baby’s temperature if they seem unwell, and whether anything you tried made a difference.


You don’t need a detailed diary. Clear observations can help your pediatrician spot patterns and ask useful follow-up questions.[UC Davis Health recommends tracking feeds, diapers, and symptoms](https://health.ucdavis.edu/conditions/pediatrics/pediatric-stomach-digestive-issues) to help describe changes in your child’s digestion. If a symptom seems urgent, contact a clinician rather than delaying care to complete your notes.


## Frequently Asked Questions


**Is it normal for my baby’s stool pattern to change?**
Yes. Stool frequency, color, and texture can vary with age and feeding method. Your baby’s usual pattern and overall wellbeing matter more than one diaper. Contact your pediatrician about hard stools, blood, or a change that persists or concerns you.


**What can I try at home to ease gas or fussiness?**
While your baby is awake, you can try gentle tummy massage, slow bicycle-leg movements, cuddling, or a warm bath. Stop if your baby seems uncomfortable. These steps may soothe your baby, but ongoing symptoms or feeding trouble deserve a conversation with your pediatrician.


**Can I give my baby water, juice, or gripe water for constipation?**
Check with your pediatrician before offering these. Breast milk or correctly prepared formula usually provides the fluids babies need during the first six months. Extra water, juice, and gripe water may not be suitable for every baby.


**Should I try a probiotic or synbiotic for my baby’s digestion?**
Ask your pediatrician before starting one. Products can contain different strains and ingredients, and research on a specific strain or concern may not apply to another product. Share the label with your clinician so they can discuss age guidance, evidence, and safety.


**Which digestive symptoms need prompt medical attention?**
Seek urgent care for green or bloody vomit, breathing trouble, or difficulty waking your baby. Contact your pediatrician promptly about fewer wet diapers, repeated vomiting or diarrhea, feeding refusal, blood in stool, or a fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher in a baby under 3 months.
